5.text: A blade of grass, a splinter of wood, or even a lump of earth taken

6.text: out of the fresh footprint of the person “doomed to anger,” may also be used

7.text: to perform upon it magic operations of the kind described.

8.text: According to another method, the performing person pretends to become

9.text: a wolf, and smears his mouth with fresh blood, proclaiming it to be the blood

10.text: of the victim. This may be compared with Incantation No. 8, d. In still

11.text: another case the performing person slaughters a reindeer in sacrifice to the

12.text: Moon, and then cuts off the head and puts it on a stake, asking the Moon to

13.text: make the victim similar to this reindeer. Then the victim is struck with palsy.

14.text: In a “spell” of the Maritime Chukchee, the performer places before the

15.text: entrance of the victim’s house a few long leaves of a species of seaweed.

16.text: The leaves are pierced with numerous holes, and therefore may serve as a

17.text: net, in the meshes of which the soul of the victim is captured. This may

18.text: be compared with an analogous action by the keˊlet.¹

19.text: But the most characteristic of all the “spells” used by the Chukchee are

20.text: the artificial creations, which are materialized, and then sent to destroy the

21.text: enemy. The same peculiar conception is to be met with among the American

23.text: The idea of such “spells” is so familiar to the Chukchee, that they try

24.text: to represent even the malevolent incantation as something likewise materialized.

25.text: For instance, in the tale of “The Scabby Shaman,” Rɪˊntew catches the malign

26.text: incantations of all his enemies, one by one, and ties them up separately in

27.text: a number of mittens. In the morning he distributes the mittens among the

28.text: baffled would-be wizards, and tells them in turn, “These are your words, —

29.text: and these are yours, — and these, yours.”³

30.text: A “spell,” once materialized, must be sent immediately in search of the

31.text: victim. It may, however, be intercepted and made ineffectual by some magic

32.text: power greater than that of its particular owner. Then it may be appropriated

33.text: by the victor, and, indeed, it will insist on being appropriated by him and sent

34.text: against its former owner. If rejected by the new wizard, it will, notwithstanding,

35.text: of its own accord, go back to its former owner and retaliate on him for its failure.

36.text: Thus I mentioned in the preceding chapter the image of such a “spell”

37.text: which was intercepted by the shaman Scratching-Woman, and then appropriated

38.text: by him for his own use. Similar ideas are to be found in the folk-lore of

39.text: civilized peoples. Thus the demons mastered by a wizard are said to clamor

40.text: constantly for more work, and that of a character harmful to others. If they
